opening.headline: To prevent incidents where agents send emails to customers without confirmation, we explain where confirmation points should be placed before difficult-to-revert steps.
body: Let's say you have a flow that automatically sends a settlement notification email to your business partner when a new file is uploaded. If an email containing an incorrect amount is sent out without confirmation, the sent email cannot be returned. The speed of automation actually increased the damage.

In this class, we'll look at what actions are difficult to reverse and how the permission step in ChatGPT and the approval step in Gemini Enterprise workflows each require human confirmation. We then go on to outline how to simulate it before turning it on and leaving a way to revert to the version.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the purpose and location of verification points
Can distinguish steps that are difficult to reverse
You can determine whether there are enough verification points

screens.title: Autorun did something it couldn't undo first.
screens.lead: First, read the accident scene created by automation.

visual.alt: Automatic flow from detecting new files to sending mail without any confirmation and displaying warnings at the sending stage.

paragraphs: One team created a flow that calculated the amount, drafted an email, and automatically sent it to the trading partner when a new settlement file was uploaded. Normally it ran fine. Then one day, the file format changed and the wrong amount was calculated, and an email containing that amount was sent to the business partner without any confirmation.

Sent mail cannot be collected. It has already arrived in the business partner's inbox, and the damage to trust cannot be completely erased even by a correction email. A miscalculation can be corrected, but a miscalculation that has gone out cannot be corrected.
Automation needs a point where it stops and people see. This lesson covers where and how to place those points.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Of the four steps in this flow, which step can be corrected even if it is wrong and which step cannot be corrected if it is wrong? Let's follow the class and set a standard.

screens.outro: First, let me recall an experience where I stopped before running.

screens.title: Have you ever stopped before running?
screens.lead: As you select each item, the instructor's thoughts unfold. First, think about your experience and then press it. Do not enter an answer.

items.prompt: Have you ever double-checked the content with the recipient just before sending an email?
items.answer: Most people have had that experience. A person automatically stops once just before sending. Automation eliminates this pause, so it must be built into the design.

items.prompt: Have you ever hesitated before deleting a file or changing its sharing settings?
items.answer: Deleting and changing sharing settings are difficult to reverse once done, or are meaningless actions once it has already been exposed to someone. Hesitation is your body's first awareness of the danger.

items.prompt: Do you think that money transactions, such as payments or applications, can be automatically entrusted?
items.answer: Financial transactions are among the things the document cites as examples of behavior that require further review. Although it can be automated, it is safer to have human confirmation right before execution.

screens.outro: Now, let’s break down in detail which actions are difficult to reverse.

screens.title: What actions are difficult to reverse?
screens.lead: Select each tab to see what types of behavior require further review. The article gives examples in four sets.

tabs.label: send
tabs.body: The act of sending emails, messages, comments, and invitations. It affects other services and other people, and once it's gone, it can't be taken back. The previous settlement email incident is of this type. Unlike reading, sending also changes the state of the receiving end.

tabs.label: Create, Edit, Delete
tabs.body: The act of creating, editing, or deleting files or records. In particular, deletions can be difficult to recover, and edits can lose their previous state if the original is overwritten. The magnitude of risk is different from reading-only behavior.

tabs.label: Change settings
tabs.body: The act of changing account, access, sharing, and security settings. If you expand the scope of sharing, more people can see it from that moment on, and once the information has been exposed, it is difficult to retrieve it. Small settings changes can have a big impact.

tabs.label: Money and Sensitive Information
tabs.body: This is the act of making a purchase or financial transaction, and sharing sensitive personal, financial, health, or identity information. The cost of mistakes can be high and can result in legal and financial liability.

tabs.label: Judgment criteria
tabs.body: The document explains that actions that may impact service, reveal sensitive information, or are difficult to reverse may require further review. Reduce it to three questions. Will the impact go out, will sensitive information be revealed, and can it be reversed? If any of these are true, it is a candidate for a verification point.

screens.outro: Now let's see how ChatGPT uses human confirmation in the face of this behavior.

screens.title: ChatGPT's Verifier: Permission Level
screens.lead: Select the arrows to see where each of the four levels of app permissions requires human confirmation.

steps.title: Always ask
steps.body: ChatGPT asks before reading or changing app information. This is the stage with the tightest number of verification points. It is suitable for apps that are connected for the first time or apps that handle sensitive data.

steps.title: Allow read actions
steps.body: Process reads without asking, and ask before making changes. The confirmation point is placed ‘just before change’. When most of your work involves finding and summarizing information, you can reduce the number of checks while still ensuring safety before writing.

steps.title: Allow low-risk actions
steps.body: Low-risk actions can be automatically approved, while high-risk actions can require confirmation or be rejected. The system determines whether the risk is high or low, so if there is a separate policy for the account, workspace, app, or connection, that policy takes precedence.

steps.title: Allow all actions
steps.body: Perform supported actions without additional approval. The document states that this option carries high risks. It does not appear in the standard account-wide and workspace-wide selection menus, and may only appear in individual apps or connections.

steps.title: Workspace policy
steps.body: In a managed workspace, member approval prompts can be set by workspace policy. No matter how loose your personalization settings are, the more stringent the policy, the more it will be enforced. When designing your verification points, you should consider your organization's policies as well as your own settings.

screens.outro: Here's how the Gemini Enterprise workflow relies on human confirmation:

screens.title: People verification steps in the Gemini Enterprise workflow
screens.lead: Select the arrows to walk through the human intervention steps Workflow Builder provides.

visual.alt: A flow in which execution stops in the middle of a workflow and continues to the next step after receiving reviewer approval.
labels: Reviewed by: Summary of amounts, confirmation of recipients

steps.title: Human in the loop stage
steps.body: Workflow Builder provides steps that pause the execution of a workflow and require human input. You can add this type of step by expanding Human in the loop in the Add step panel. This feature is available after your administrator turns on the Workflow Builder feature toggle.

steps.title: Request info step
steps.body: Stop the workflow and ask the user one or more questions. This step is used when additional information or confirmation is needed to proceed. In the Message field, write the context of why the input is needed, and in Info to request, specify the question and input format (e.g. Short answer).

steps.title: Approval stage
steps.body: Stop the workflow and present deliverables for human review and approval. Approval is required for subsequent steps to be executed. This step is best placed as a checkpoint before actions that are difficult to reverse. Set what information you want to show to reviewers.

steps.title: Find stuck execution
steps.body: When a run reaches the human intervention stage, it is paused and appears in the Runs tab with a Needs Review status. Reviewers can use this list to find and process runs that require confirmation.

steps.title: Limitations of administrator policy
steps.body: The actions and tools that agents and workflows created with Workflow Builder can use are limited to the data connectors, tools, and permissions that your administrator has in place. The human verification phase and administrator control work together at different layers.

screens.outro: If you put in a confirmation point, you need to check it before turning it on and also have a way to revert it.

screens.title: Preview and revert versions
screens.lead: Select the two states alternately to compare the inspection before turning it on and the safety net after turning it on.

states.label: Before turning on: Simulation
states.body: Select Start simulation in the Preview tab to realistically simulate the workflow. The way you give input or answer questions is the same as in actual execution. When you're done, you'll see a summary, which you can expand to see the actions, reasoning, and output of each step. It is suitable for checking before turning on whether it really stops at the approval stage and whether the output of each stage is as intended.

states.label: After turning it on: Revert version
states.body: Workflows can be saved as drafts or turned on. Even after it's turned on, you can create new versions and verify them without touching the running version. You can select a previous version from Version history and turn it on, so you can go back to the previous version when needed. It is a second safety net when operations present issues that the verification point missed.

screens.outro: Now let's apply what we've learned to the settlement email example.

screens.title: Commentary: Adding a confirmation point to the vendor settlement email workflow
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of fixing the problem by adding confirmation points to the flow where the first accident occurred. Select the arrow to move on.

steps.title: Take a look at the original flow
steps.body: The original flow had four steps: detect new file, calculate amount, draft mail, and send mail. The starting point is to consider one by one which of these steps are incorrect and cannot be corrected.

steps.title: reversible steps
steps.body: Detecting a new file is a start condition for read nature. Calculating the amount is an internal process, so even if it is wrong, you can just do it again. You can even edit your email draft before sending it. You can leave these three steps automatic.

steps.title: an irreversible step
steps.body: Sending emails affects external business partners, and once sent, it cannot be reversed. Candidate confirmation point is just before dispatch. This is because even if there are incorrect values ​​in the previous step, they can be filtered out here.

steps.title: Approval stage design
steps.body: Place an Approval step between drafting the email and sending it. The information to be shown to the reviewer is a summary of the amount for each customer and a list of recipients. Reviewers should be able to decide whether to approve or not just by looking at the number and destination.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: One verification point was sufficient. If we had to rely on calculating amounts and writing drafts for approval, the benefits of automation would have been lost. The balance is to have people stop only at the one point where there is no turning back, right before sending.

screens.outro: Since I have included confirmation points, I will explain the inspection and reversal before turning it on.

screens.title: Explanation: Check before turning on and revert if problems occur.
screens.lead: The instructor explains the procedure for putting the modified workflow into operation. Select the arrows and follow them step by step.

steps.title: Confirm freeze with simulation
steps.body: Start the simulation in the Preview tab to make sure it really stops at the Approval stage. This confirmation is most important. I thought I had added the approval step, but if the setting is missing, the accident still happens.

steps.title: Check output with summary
steps.body: At the end of the simulation, expand the summary that appears to see if the actions, inferences, and outputs of each step are as intended. Also try entering the conditions that caused the accident, such as when the file format has changed.

steps.title: Confirm and turn on
steps.body: Turn on the overhauled workflow. When turned on, existing drafts become live versions and new drafts are created. You can also just save it as Save version only before turning it on.

steps.title: If there is a problem, go to the previous version
steps.body: If you find any problems during operation, select the previous version from Version history and turn it on. When you turn off the live version, the status changes to Draft. Knowing that there is a way to revert allows you to try new versions quickly.

steps.title: Privilege starts narrowly
steps.body: Permissions are treated the same way. Start with reading and expand by checking only the areas that require writing. The sufficiency of a confirmation point can be judged in three ways: check, approval, and revert.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: There are people in front of writing, sending, and deleting.
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.

paragraphs: The speed of automation is a strength, but irreversible actions are a weakness. Place a human confirmation point before actions that have external impact, such as sending emails, deleting files, changing settings, or making payments.

Confirmation can be done in two ways. Permission settings ask before changes, such as Always ask or Allow read actions, and workflow requires approval at the Approval stage. Whether there are enough verification points is judged by whether all steps that are difficult to reverse are covered and whether unnecessary steps are blocked.
Finally, simulate it before turning it on, and leave a way to revert to the previous version after you turn it on.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Put a check in one place that is difficult to reverse, and leave the steps that can be reversed automatically.

checks.q: Which of the following steps has the greatest need for a confirmation point before automatic execution?
options: Steps to calculate the customer settlement amount
Steps to write an email draft sentence
Steps to send settlement information emails to business partners
Steps to detect that a new file has been uploaded
checks.explain: Sending mail has an external impact and cannot be reversed, so there needs to be a human confirmation point just before execution.

wrong.0: Calculating the amount is an internal task that can be reversed, so you can leave it automatic.
wrong.1: Drafting is low-risk because you can edit it before sending it out.
wrong.3: File detection is a read-only startup condition and has no external influence.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Put your newly created workflows in the right order when putting them into production.
items: Simulate to verify that it really stops at the approval stage
In the summary, check whether the output of each step is as intended.
If a problem occurs, revert to the previous version.
checks.explain: Before turning it on, check it with simulation and summary, and if there are any problems after turning it on, there is a way to revert to the previous version.
checks.intro: Put them in order, remembering the order you learned them. Results are not recorded.

glossary.def: This is where the automatic flow stops and human review and approval occurs.
This is the step in Workflow Builder where the results must be shown to a person and approved before the next step can be executed.
A step in Workflow Builder that stops execution and prompts the user for additional information.
This is a feature that previews the workflow before turning it on to view step-by-step actions and output.

misconceptions.myth: The faster automation is done, the better.
misconceptions.fact: For actions that are difficult to reverse, confirmation is more important than speed. This is because the speed at which incorrect results are released also increases.

misconceptions.myth: It is safe only if approval is given at every step.
misconceptions.fact: If you stop at a reversible step, the benefits of automation are lost. Focus and place checkpoints before steps that are difficult to reverse.

misconceptions.myth: Since the simulation was done, there is no need for version management.
misconceptions.fact: Simulations do not represent all operating situations. Leave a way to revert to a previous version in case of operational problems.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Place confirmation points before actions that are difficult to reverse.
Confirmation is done in two ways: permission stage and approval stage.
Keep the advantage by leaving reversible steps automatic.
Leave a way to simulate and revert to a version before turning it on.
